variants.name: ActiveRecord optimistic locking
variants.implementation_notes: ActiveRecord supports optimistic locking whenever an integer lock_version column is present: each update increments the column and the locking facilities make the later of two instances raise ActiveRecord::StaleObjectError when its UPDATE matches no row; the check also runs on destroy. The column name is configurable (self.locking_column = :lock_person) and the facility can be switched off globally (ActiveRecord::Base.lock_optimistically = false). Since the exception carries no merge data, resolution lives in your rescue block.
variants.code_sketch:
p1 = Account.find(1)
p2 = Account.find(1)            # same lock_version loaded
p1.update(balance: 0)           # succeeds, lock_version 1 -> 2
begin
  p2.update(balance: 100)       # UPDATE ... WHERE id=1 AND lock_version=1
rescue ActiveRecord::StaleObjectError
  p2.reload                     # then merge or report the conflict
end
pitfalls: Across web requests the lock_version must be round-tripped (a hidden form field), otherwise every request loads fresh state and the check never fires.
update_column/update_all/update_columns bypass callbacks and the version check entirely - a silent lost update.
Serialising a model to JSON for an API drops lock_version unless it is added explicitly, leaving the client unable to send the token back.

variants.name: Sequel optimistic_locking plugin
variants.implementation_notes: Sequel ships the same mechanism as a plugin - 'a simple database-independent locking mechanism to ensure that concurrent updates do not override changes' - enabled per model with plugin :optimistic_locking: the lock column is added to the WHERE clause of the guarded update and a save that matches no row raises instead of overwriting. The column defaults to lock_version and can be renamed; dataset-level bulk updates bypass it, as with ActiveRecord.
variants.code_sketch:
class Account < Sequel::Model
  plugin :optimistic_locking      # adds lock_version to the WHERE clause
end
a = Account[1]; b = Account[1]
a.update(balance: 0)
b.update(balance: 100)   # guarded update matches no row -> raises
pitfalls: The plugin is per model: forgetting it on one class leaves that model unguarded while the schema still looks protected.
Dataset updates (Account.where(...).update(...)) and multi_insert do not go through the plugin's instance save path.
The lock column must exist and be non-null on the table; adding the plugin without the migration fails at save time.
